newsitem.title: NORWAY: Saga moves closer to Santa Fe takeover.
newsitem.headline: Saga moves closer to Santa Fe takeover.

text.p: Norwegian oil company Saga Petroleum ASA said on Tuesday its supervisory board had approved a takeover of Kuwaiti-owned North Sea exploration group Santa Fe Exploration Ltd.
Final confirmation that KPC had accepted the deal was expected soon.
The supervisory board met with Saga's management on Monday night to discuss the acquisition from state-owned Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC).
"Saga Petrolem confirms that the company's supervisory board has approved the proposal for an agreement to buy North Sea Holdings Ltd (Santa Fe)," a statement from Saga said.
"Saga will hold a news conference as soon as final clarification on the takeover is ready. The company expects a quick clarification," it said.
Market sources had expected Saga to make an announcement on Tuesday following the board meeting and after its shares were suspended from trading on the Oslo bourse a day earlier.

Market speculation indicated Saga had clinched the deal at $1.2 billion (7.72 billion crowns). If confirmed, the acquisition will be the second largest by a Norwegian company following Kvaerner's takeover of British conglomerate Trafalgar House plc in April for 8.9 billion crowns.
Analysts were downbeat on a takeover at that level, saying it represented a premium of 50 percent on even the most bullish estimates of Santa Fe's value at between $700 and $800 million.
It could slash up to 20 percent off Saga's share price, which stood at 105.50 crowns before trading was suspended on Monday, they said.
"Saga will have to work hard to justify the price. I expect the share price to be cut by about 20 crowns," said one analyst.

Gundi Royle at Morgan Stanley & Co said: "Our indicative valuation would be some $700-750 million, and so a price of $1 billion (based on reserves for sale of 150 million of barrels of oil equivalent), would be exceptional."

Saga has long recognised a need to diversify out of the Norwegian sector of the North Sea, where about 95 percent of its hydrocarbon production is concentrated, to maintain its reserve base and remain competitive.
A move into the British sector, which is geographically close to Norway and has a similar geology, would also allow a certain amount of spin-off from its Norwegian operations.

But higher oil prices, interest in the area West of Shetland, where the last sizable oil discoveries were made, and an attractive fiscal policy has recently attracted renewed interest into the mature area.
"It was the most intensive auctions in this sector that I've ever seen, the whole indistry was bidding," said a London-based analyst.
U.S.-based Conoco, a unit of E.I. Du Pont De Nemours and Co, was one participant in the bidding round.
